sleepers.name: Terrance Ferguson
sleepers.blurb: The 2nd year TE is probably buried in your fantasy platform's ADP but his potential upside in this Rams offense should not be slept on. He led all TEs in 20+ air yard targets last year in a specialized role as the team's downfield threat. Sean McVay runs a ridiculous amount of 2 and 3-TE sets where Ferguson functions essentially as the team's slot WR. We project him as the 3rd option in this passing offense behind Davante Adams and Puka Nacua with a chance to become a sneaky TE option in 2026.

sleepers.name: Malik Willis
sleepers.blurb: With the ADP market getting sharper year over year, it’s getting more difficult to find late-round QB upside. As a passer, we are not sure what Malik Willis can do, especially with these weapons. However, we know rushing at the QB position is a cheat code in fantasy, and Willis has serious upside as a mobile QB. Since 2024, he’s averaging 6.6 rushing points per game, making him an intriguing QB2 with upside. It is a small sample size, but in four games where Willis took the majority of the snaps over the last two years, his rushing stat lines are 9/60/2, 10/44/0, 6/73/1, and 6/41/0.

sleepers.name: Tyler Shough
sleepers.blurb: New Orleans went with Spencer Rattler to open the 2025 campaign, and to no one’s surprise, the Saints went 1-7 to open the year. From Week 9 on, the Saints were a respectable 5-4 under Shough, who banked five QB1 weekly finishes in his nine starts. Kellen Moore’s offenses are always up-tempo and ranking among the league leaders in pace of play, so Shough and the Saints offense are on the short list of teams capable of finishing inside the top-five in overall play volume. When you have a mobile QB like Shough, who is now throwing to stud Chris Olave, top-10 NFL Draft pick Jordyn Tyson, and free agent signee Travis Etienne out of the backfield, it’s not hard to see a world where Shough outperforms his ADP. The Saints also have the second-easiest strength of schedule in the NFL, and they play 10 dome games in 2026.

sleepers.name: Rico Dowdle
sleepers.blurb: The Steelers are once again one of fantasy football’s ambiguous RB rooms entering 2026. After Jaylen Warren and Kenneth Gainwell both ended up being great values in drafts a year ago, we are interested in taking shots on the Steelers’ backs as long as ADPs are held in check. Warren was good last year, and it is certainly possible he wins the job, but it’s important to remember that for the first time in forever, we have a new staff in Pittsburgh. Warren comes from the Tomlin regime, while Dowdle was brought in via free agency this offseason. Back in 2024, when Dowdle played for Mike McCarthy in Dallas, he took over the RB1 job and finished as a solid RB2 for fantasy. Last season in Carolina, we saw him steal that job from Chuba Hubbard, and Dowdle has now banked back-to-back seasons with 280+ total opportunities and 4.6 yards per carry. Both Pittsburgh backs are good bets at cost, but we are leaning towards Rico, given his familiarity with McCarthy.

sleepers.name: Jonathon Brooks
sleepers.blurb: Call him an international man of mystery as we have little on-field evidence through two injury-plagued seasons that Brooks can be a lead back in the NFL. However, the backfield situation in Carolina might be more up for grabs than fantasy managers realize. The slow-footed Chuba Hubbard had zero runs of 15+ yards as Rico Dowdle usurped him after the first month of the season and saw a whopping 36% of the team's total rush attempts and targets from Week 5 on. Brooks can step into a bigger role in 2026 with Rico departed and his pass-catching profile from his days at Texas should boost his upside in your mind. For now, his ADP is tame which screams sleeper material in your drafts.

sleepers.name: Blake Corum
sleepers.blurb: For the last couple of seasons, the Rams have hinted at more of a committee approach to ease the workload on Kyren Williams, and down the stretch last season, we finally saw that come to fruition with Corum siphoning off 145 rush attempts to Kyren’s 259. We are still projecting Williams to maintain his RB1 role in 2026, but it is possible that the gap is tighter than it was a season ago after Corum bested his teammate in yards per carry, explosive rush rate, and missed tackles forced per attempt. If this happens to be more of an even split, Corum is a sneaky value later in drafts. Even if Kyren keeps his bell cow role, Corum is one of fantasy’s top-tier insurance backs tied to one of the best offenses in football.

sleepers.name: Jacory Croskey-Merritt
sleepers.blurb: Bill Croskey mania took over last year and it can be tough remembering where we've landed since. He profiles as the early downs back on an offense that should be in a number of shootouts to start the season. When looking at the Commanders’ RB depth chart, it features the inefficient Rachaad White, and Day 3 rookie, Kaytron Allen. White should have a receiving role as part of a committee at a minimum, but there is also a world that exists where JCM wins the RB1 job entering the season. He is the most explosive back and recent beat reports this off-season are emphasizing JCM being in on passing downs.Given that his ADP is dirt cheap, you can tack him onto the end of your bench as your RB4 with virtually zero risk.

sleepers.name: Jordan Mason
sleepers.blurb: Mason might be seen as an afterthought in your drafts but he projects to be the early down thumper and goal-line back. His efficiency metrics were way better than you might remember from last year ranking 9th in rush success rate, 4th in percentage of 10+ yard runs, and 9th in forced missed tackle rate. Aaron Jones Sr. will mix in on passing downs but his injury issues and age declines have him 2nd in the pecking order of preferred Minnesota RBs. Kyler Murray at QB can hopefully restores some of the up-tempo, high-play volume we’ve been accustomed to from Kevin O'Connell offenses the previous three seasons. Mason is a late round pick likely forgotten by the rest of your leaguemates.

sleepers.name: Quentin Johnston
sleepers.blurb: The Chargers' offense should look a lot different in 2026 with new OC Mike McDaniel now calling plays. Their roster moves suggest we will see plenty of multi-TE sets, so figuring out which Charger WRs are playing in 2WR sets is going to be crucial for predicting fantasy success in this WR room. Johnston makes a lot of sense in that role given his size, speed, and ability to play on the perimeter. Since that forgettable rookie season, Johnston has improved year-over-year in fantasy points per game and yards per reception as a player who seems to be figuring it out in the NFL. With Justin Herbert under center in a scheme that could unlock plenty of efficiency, Johnston is worth a pick in the later rounds of drafts as a potential WR3/FLEX with the capability to provide your roster some ceiling performances.

sleepers.name: Josh Downs
sleepers.blurb: The problem for Josh Downs in fantasy over the years has been a lack of playing time in 2WR sets. The talent has never been a question, but it is hard to get overly excited about a slot-only player in today’s NFL. Moving forward, Downs’ role could grow in 2026 as an every down player with Michael Pittman now in Pittsburgh. The Colts’ depth at WR is relatively weak, and when you consider that Alec Pierce has never been a high-volume WR throughout his collegiate or NFL career, Downs could really pile up volume as Indy’s top WR target earner. You can snag him as your WR4 or WR5 in drafts with next to no risk, considering his late ADP in the double-digit rounds.

sleepers.name: Parker Washington
sleepers.blurb: If you checked out during the back half of last year, you probably missed what Parker Washington did down the stretch. From Week 9 on, Washington’s 17-game pace was 77 catches, over 1,200 yards, and 7.5 TDs. He even went 7/107/1 in the playoffs against Buffalo. The previous regime never really gave him a shot to be an every-down player, but under Liam Cohen, Washington was a key contributor down the stretch after Travis Hunter landed on IR. Looking ahead to 2026, the Jaguars’ WR room is one of the most difficult to project in the league. Brian Thomas Jr. is a wild card, Jakobi Meyers remains a serviceable NFL WR, and Travis Hunter’s role remains a complete question mark. That uncertainty will keep Washington’s ADP in check. As long as that is the case, we don’t mind taking a swing on a player who was highly efficient in this scheme over a pretty decent sample a year ago.

sleepers.name: De'Zhaun Stribling
sleepers.blurb: The 49ers unexpectedly took Stribling with the first pick of the second round and we immediately started scratching our heads: "What do they know that we don't?!" The Ole Miss product has the size/speed combination we look for at the NFL level and the drum beat this off-season has been nothing but positive for Stribling. With Ricky Pearsall out for the season with another injury, there is room for the rookie to start right away in 2WR sets alongside Mike Evans for the 49ers. Even with SF bringing back Deebo Samuel, the rookie is an intriguing flier at the end of your drafts on an offense that we desperately want pieces of in 2026. You can throw a dart late and stash him with next to no risk.

sleepers.name: Isaiah Likely
sleepers.blurb: After signing a 3-year deal to reunite with John Harbaugh in New York, Likely now finds himself the 4th highest paid TE in the league in terms of per year average ($13.33 million). We have seen great moments from him as he averaged 12.5 PPR fantasy points per game in nine games without Mark Andrews in Baltimore. Every trusted Giants source has echoed that Likely has been Jaxson Dart's #1 target in camp with Malik Nabers out and likely (see what we did there) will be the No. 2 when he returns. Very few TEs carry this type of upside this late in your drafts so swing away!

sleepers.name: Chig Okonkwo
sleepers.blurb: The Commanders added Stefon Diggs but as it stands, the WR depth chart behind Terry McLaurin is weak with guys like Treylon Burks, Dyami Brown, and third-round rookie Antonio Williams as possible contributors. Enter Chig Okonkwo, who signed a three-year deal in free agency with almost $17M guaranteed. It is certainly possible he is the 2nd or 3rd option in the pass game, and given his athletic profile, we are willing to take shots in drafts as a late-round option.

sleepers.name: Greg Dulcich
sleepers.blurb: Greg D! That’s right, baby. The man with the luscious locks and mustache has made the official Sleepers list. Now, let’s not get too crazy. You do not need to be drafting Greg D in standard 10-team leagues or most 12-team leagues, but if you play in a deeper league and are looking for a guy you can snag well into the double-digit rounds if you are punting the position, Dulcich is worth a look. The Dolphins have very little talent at the WR position after cutting Tyreek Hill, trading away Jaylen Waddle, and moving on from Darren Waller. Dulcich is likely to play as an every-down TE, and he is quietly coming off an efficient 12.9 yards per reception in 2025. We obviously aren’t projecting him as a top-12 guy for the season, but it would not be surprising at all to see him bank multiple TE1 weeks thanks to his athletic ability after the catch.

breakouts.name: Jaxson Dart
breakouts.blurb: The New York Football Giants traded up into the first round in 2025 to get their potential QB of the future in Ole Miss Rebel Jaxson Dart. And I think we can say, the gamble paid off. The first two games were questionable as he took over for Russell Wilson (remember that experiment?!), but he settled in quickly, changing the identity in New York. The QB16 on the season finished with almost 2,300 yards passing, but we all know that Dart’s rushing ability is his true calling card. He piled up 487 yards on the ground in 14 games (the third most among QBs) and nine TDs (the third most in NFL history by a rookie QB). You cannot ignore the elephant in the room - Dart runs with a kind of reckless abandon that makes you cover your eyes and cringe, consistently nervous that every rush may be his last. Be that as it may, Dart’s upside in his sophomore year is sky high, and to get that rushing upside as late as the range of QB8 to QB10 off the draft board makes him worth his weight in gold. Add in the fact that John Harbaugh is the new HC in town, and you might have a league winner on your hands with Dart, even if it takes time to get Malik Nabers back. Let’s learn to slide, though, Jaxson!

breakouts.name: Trevor Lawrence
breakouts.blurb: After wig-gate of 2026, it is time to fully consider Trevor Lawrence a thing. The fantasy community has gone back and forth during Lawrence’s tenure in the NFL, debating whether or not he was actually good at football, and some people are still not accepting it, even after his QB4 finish last year. He was one of six QBs who threw for over 4,000 yards, and his end-of-season run, fantasy-wise, was one championships were made of. Oh, and may I remind you he also runs? He managed 359 yards with his legs (10th), nine rushing TDs (tied for second most), and 39 rushing first downs (second most). We are big fans of the Jaguars offense and what Liam Coen is doing in Jacksonville, and we see a world where the Horse Child comes out of the gate galloping in 2026.

breakouts.name: Kenneth Walker
breakouts.blurb: The Kansas City Chiefs gave Ken Bone a three-year, $43 million contract for one clear reason: their RB situation in 2025 was not one that dreams were made of. A backfield made up of aging Kareem Hunt, Isiah Pacheco, and Brashard Smith managed just over 1,200 yards on the ground, pushing Mahomes to scramble (422 yards rushing) and ultimately go down to injury. The team's total yards on the ground? The eighth fewest in the league. Enter the Super Bowl MVP to save the day! Walker should get tons of opportunity; we anticipate less running from Mahomes recovering from that ACL tear, Travis Kelce is not any younger, and Rashee Rice is…who knows. The Chiefs' offensive identity could run through Walker this year, his ADP is incredibly manageable, and the depth chart is far from intimidating. Color Mike ecstatic.

breakouts.name: Omarion Hampton
breakouts.blurb: What a tease of a season we got from rookie Omarion Hampton a year ago. He had 314 yards rushing and 136 yards receiving before he went down to an ankle injury Week 5. He returned in Week 14 and gave us three out of four weeks as a top-20 RB before he sat out the final week of the season. When he was on the field, we saw the flashes that the Chargers saw when drafting Hampton 22nd overall in 2025. Now, Hampton gets a healthy offensive line, with both Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater back and a new OC in Mike McDaniel, who loves to lean on a featured back when the situation presents (ahem, De’Von Achane). Behind Hampton, we are looking at Keaton Mitchell, Kimani Vidal, and FB Alec Ingold, presenting an opportunity for him to be quite the workhorse in Los Angeles.

breakouts.name: Bhayshul Tuten
breakouts.blurb: Tuten spent the majority of 2025 bottled up behind Travis Etienne Jr., with only a 25% rushing share to Etienne’s 70%. That said, Tuten was efficient with his scoring when he got the opportunity. He turned his seven attempts inside the 5-yard line into five TDs, whereas Etienne was nowhere as successful, only cashing in twice on 12 attempts. With Etienne off to New Orleans, Tuten gets the keys to the Jag(uars), and he is getting overlooked in drafts as a potential RB1. We see the Jacksonville offense as one to target in 2026, and a team that had 22 rushing TDs in 2025 (tied for the fourth-most) will need to hand the ball off to someone. With CROD (Chris Rodriguez Jr.) and LeQuint Allen Jr. rounding out the depth chart, our money is on Tuten to be that guy.

breakouts.name: Christian Watson
breakouts.blurb: If you have ever had Christian Watson on your fantasy team, you know the roller coaster ride well. Seemingly prone to injuries, you could never drop the guy, because when on the field, he was always a threat for a big play. He played ten games last season and was the WR13 or better in four of them, including a fabulous WR4 finish in Championship week against Baltimore. He finished the year fifth in yards per route run and averaged 17.5 yards per reception. It was scarier to roster Watson last season when the WR room was as packed as Costco on a Saturday afternoon, but now there is some breathing room. Romeo Doubs is in New England, Dontayvion Wicks is an Eagle, and Matthew Golden is still Matthew Golden. Target-wise, the battle looks to be between Jayden Reed, Tucker Kraft, and Watson, and even if Watson gets the short end of that stick, he is on a great offense with a solid QB, and going late enough in drafts that he could be your WR3.

breakouts.name: Carnell Tate
breakouts.blurb: Welcome in the fourth overall pick to the breakout conversation. And how could you not? Tennessee made a strong statement by drafting an alpha for second-year QB Cam Ward this year, and we can assume the organization has a plan for the WR out of Ohio State. Even with the addition of Wan’Dale Robinson, the depth chart is sparse, setting up Tate to be the guy. The only concern with drafting him is whether or not Cam Ward can make the leap to make Tate’s ADP a steal. We think he can.

breakouts.name: Tetairoa McMillan
breakouts.blurb: The reigning Offensive Rookie of the Year is coming off a WR17 season where he had just over 1,000 yards and seven TDs. There were obviously some ups and downs - fantasy finishes as low as WR108 (!) and as high as WR1 - but perhaps it is that exact roller coaster that is keeping his ADP manageable. We are ready for that patented second-year WR breakout on a team that has not changed drastically when it comes to offensive weapons. McMillan had a 25% target share in 2025, the 14th-highest among WRs, and with no massive draft-day additions beyond third-round draft pick Chris Brazzell, we anticipate the same this year. If Bryce Young improves again this year and McMillan catches a few more TDs, you will be extremely happy with your investment.

breakouts.name: Colston Loveland
breakouts.blurb: What else is there to say about Mr. Lovelaaaand? He finished the 2025 season with 82 targets and was on an upward trajectory. The final two weeks of the regular season gave us a glimpse at what he could be moving forward - 10 and 13 targets, close to 100 yards receiving each game, and each with a receiving TD. There are a lot of mouths to feed in Chicago, but Loveland proved his trustworthiness in the playoffs, as Caleb Williams went to him in the biggest moments. If Caleb can complete just a few more passes, we are looking at a bump in Loveland’s production. With TEs, we are great or late over here at Ballers HQ, and the difference in ADP between the McBride/Bowers duo and Loveland is significant enough to set him up as a potential value in a breakout season.

breakouts.name: Harold Fannin Jr.
breakouts.blurb: Fannin exploded in the second half of 2025, as he was the TE12 or better in four out of the final five weeks he played - including a TE1 and a TE2 finish! Look, the QB situation in Cleveland is still murky at best, but there is even more opportunity for Fannin with the departure of David Njoku. He leaves behind 48 targets, and we know that even a bad offense can give us fantasy gold - he was targeted 12 times in the red zone, more than any WR on the team. The team did add rookies Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion, but we see a world where Fannin meets or exceeds his 21.4% target share.

busts.name: Matthew Stafford
busts.blurb: Scared of regression? Listen, we get it: it is tough to repeat 46 passing TDs and an MVP season. Let this stat put his career into context: through 17(!) seasons, Stafford has never put up back-to-back seasons of 27+ TDs ever. Those goal-line TDs we were so used to seeing for Davante Adams could easily shift in 2026 as McVay puts his offensive imagination to the test. We do not consider him an every week start and thus not someone we are leaving our drafts with unless he is paired with another QB.

busts.name: Patrick Mahomes
busts.blurb: This one hurts. We love Mahomes. Who doesn’t?! He is still viewed as one of, if not the, best QBs in the league, but for the game we play, 2026 may not be the year for Mahomes to be a difference-making fantasy QB. He is coming off a multi-ligament ACL injury, and the Chiefs did very little to add to their pass-catching corps. With Travis Kelce another year older and Kenneth Walker now in town to take the load off Mahomes, we don’t see him separating in a meaningful way for fantasy, especially if he is not going to scramble the way he did a year ago, coming off this serious knee injury. There is a chance his name value keeps his ADP too high for our liking.

busts.name: Chuba Hubbard
busts.blurb: There were a couple of alarming truths that emerge after we reviewed Chuba's 2025 season. He was usurped by Rico Dowdle, he had one total carry inside the 5-yard line and no runs of 15+ yards on the season. Yikes! Jonathon Brooks' rise over the summer is certainly making us nervous about selecting the 27-year-old as the Panthers' RB1 in our drafts. He could begin the year as the lead in the backfield but there are routes where he ends up in a full timeshare or is surpassed on the depth chart at some point. That is not a profile we want to bet on in the 7th round on a team projected for just 6.5 wins on the season.

busts.name: RJ Harvey
busts.blurb: Harvey’s fantasy production was solid in 2025, especially for a rookie. However, most of that production was unsustainable as he was fortunate in the TD department, finding the end zone 12 times. With J.K. Dobbins back on the roster and the Broncos selecting Jonah Coleman in the NFL Draft, Harvey is likely to remain as part of a committee, which means he will need to rely on efficiency to get the job done in fantasy. That is where the concerns come in. Harvey ranked 46th out of 48 qualified backs in rushing yards over expected per attempt; he was 32nd in success rate, and he averaged a pedestrian 3.7 yards per carry despite playing behind one of the best lines in football. We would like to be optimistic about a Year 2 breakout, but the warning signs are there in a crowded offense that just added another mouth to feed in Jaylen Waddle.

busts.name: Malik Nabers
busts.blurb: It stinks being down on one of the most electrifying WRs in the league, but this is all about injury with Malik Nabers. He is coming off an ACL reconstruction and a meniscus repair and required a secondary procedure in the spring to aid in his recovery. Because of this lengthy rehab, we are not expecting him to return to form until the middle of the season, so with his ADP likely to remain elevated because of the name value, he is a tough sell early in drafts where the opportunity cost is so high.

busts.name: DJ Moore
busts.blurb: Is there a world where Josh Allen unlocks DJ Moore for one more elite fantasy season? Of course, it’s certainly possible, but this Bills offense has been great without having one WR make a difference for fantasy, as they generally spread things out in the pass game and feed James Cook in the red zone. Perhaps that changes with the trade of Moore, but there are also some warning signs on Moore as a player at this stage of his career. Historically speaking, 29-year-old WRs changing teams have not been a great bet in fantasy, and Moore is coming off career lows in receptions, receiving yards, yards per route run, and missed tackles forced. The allure of Josh Allen’s WR1 probably keeps his ADP at a range where we’re fine passing in drafts this year.

busts.name: Courtland Sutton
busts.blurb: Sutton has been a great value in drafts in back-to-back seasons, finishing as the WR13 in both 2024 and 2025. Unfortunately, the numbers and the changing situation suggest that is probably not repeatable. Denver traded for Jaylen Waddle before the NFL Draft, and he is certainly going to steal some volume. That is a scary proposition for Sutton, who could become a TD-or-bust option in 2026. The veteran also turns 31 later this year, and that is usually around the age where we start to see non-elite WRs trend down in terms of their efficiency.

busts.name: Oronde Gadsden
busts.blurb: After he burst onto the scene with a monster 4-game stretch as a rookie, Oronde Gadsden II has slowly faded away from fantasy relevance. While touting a young TE can be tempting, the arrival of Mike McDaniel and multiple TEs in free agency shifted much of the optimism. On Sleeper's platform, he looks like a glaring overdraft candidate. The Chargers have reimagined their offensive philosophy and Gadsden has not been consistently working with the starters throughout camp. Let someone else in your league take a shot as there are many other young, athletic TEs we would rather bet on.

busts.name: Jake Ferguson
busts.blurb: After gathering eight TDs and over 100 targets in 2025, you might think Ferguson is a sneaky target in 2026. We feel the exact opposite as a deeper dive into his season reveals a rough final 3 months. He failed to hit double-digit fantasy points from Week 8 on gathering just a 13% target share in that span. He is at best the 3rd target in this offense trailing CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. If you want to play the TD roulette game every week, he can have his moments. However, there are many other TE options available who should provide a better guaranteed weekly floor than Turd Ferg.

values.name: Brock Purdy
values.blurb: It feels like Purdy’s fantasy fame remains overlooked despite an unreal finish in the fantasy playoffs. He is consistently a TD outlier and adds enough on the ground to give you a weekly floor. The 49ers are double-digit home favorites in Weeks 2 and 3, where you can expect them to sport the highest implied totals. Get ahead of your league mates by either grabbing Purdy as your QB2 and waiting to plug him in for those contests.

values.name: Dak Prescott
values.blurb: The Rodney Dangerfield of fantasy football continues to be disrespected by fantasy managers. The passing volume is consistent, and the team throws inside the red zone, as evidenced by his 13 passing TDs inside the 5-yard line. If you pass on the elite QBs early in your drafts, let your league mates spend mid-round draft capital knowing Dak is available in the later rounds as a “backstop” for your team. Dak finished as a top-12 QB every single full season of his career, and we expect that trend to continue again in 2026.

values.name: Derrick Henry
values.blurb: Ageists have been trying to sink the King for years, and yet it feels like he grows stronger and stronger. Maybe the hate fuels him! As the lead back on a team projected for a league-leading 11.5 wins, why is Derrick Henry so low in ADP this year? Anyone want a shot at double-digit TDs in the third round? Our projections for the 32-year-old remain strong as he remains one of the great outliers of fantasy football.

values.name: Javonte Williams
values.blurb: After being one of the steals of the 2025 fantasy season, Javonte’s ADP is quite palatable in 2026. He signed a three-year extension in Dallas, and the backfield competition behind him is nonexistent. Finding a workhorse RB in the fourth round coming off an RB1 season is a rare event. It would not be shocking to see him repeat 300+ opportunities and double-digit TDs.

values.name: Cam Skattebo
values.blurb: Is he a little crazy? Sure, but we like that from our fantasy RBs and it seems like Skatt is still being punished too much for last season's injury as he looks like a great value according to our Value Scout tool. He should handle a three-down workload and operate as the clear goal-line back on a Giants team we like to take a step forward in 2026. Consider him a strong RB2 with the type of high-end ceiling to finish as a top 10 back.

values.name: D'Andre Swift
values.blurb: Daaaaa Bears! Year 1 of the Ben Johnson era was a smashing success with Chicago ranking ninth in both points per game and yards per play en route to their first double-digit win season since 2018! D'Andre Swift is coming off a 2025 campaign in which he set career highs in rushing yards (1,087) and rushing TDs (9) behind one of the better offensive lines in football, and the Bears didn't add any competition to the backfield. Kyle Monangai will see some work, but Swift should lead the backfield yet again for a team that should win plenty of games and put up plenty of points. He's finished as a top-24 fantasy RB in six straight seasons, making him a rock solid pick as your RB2 in fantasy drafts.

values.name: J.K. Dobbins
values.blurb: It feels like we are in "de ja vu" again as the Broncos backfield remains an ADP mystery like it was in 2025. Dobbins was re-signed to a 2-year extension this off-season and yet here we are again with question marks surrounding his stranglehold on the backfield. RJ Harvey will certainly mix in on passing downs but Dobbins projects as the lead ball carrier behind the NFL's best offensive line. The fact you can get a starting RB for a team coming off a 14-win season this late in your drafts screams value!

values.name: Jaylen Waddle
values.blurb: In March, the Broncos traded for the soon-to-be 28-year-old WR sending a 1st rounder to Miami. Since then, Sean Payton has not stopped gushing about Waddle all off-season saying he “walks on water” with his traits. Waddle remains in his prime as his per-route metrics from 2025 (2.42 YPRR) remind you that he is still a special player. Expect a ton of easy "layup targets" as Bo Nix has led the NFL in screen attempts over the last two seasons. He is the perfect addition to this Broncos offense and yet, his draft price remains far too cheap for a player we've seen finish inside the top-20 twice in his career.

values.name: Parker Washington
values.blurb: If you checked out during the back half of last year, you probably missed what Parker Washington did down the stretch. From Week 9 on, Washington’s 17-game pace was 77 catches, over 1,200 yards, and 7.5 TDs. He even went 7/107/1 in the playoffs against Buffalo. The previous regime never really gave him a shot to be an every-down player, but under Liam Cohen, Washington was a key contributor down the stretch after Travis Hunter landed on IR. Looking ahead to 2026, the Jaguars’ WR room is one of the most difficult to project in the league. Brian Thomas Jr. is a wild card, Jakobi Meyers remains a serviceable NFL WR, and Travis Hunter’s role remains a complete question mark. As long as that is the case, we don’t mind taking a swing on a player who was highly efficient in this scheme over a pretty decent sample a year ago.

values.name: Terry McLaurin
values.blurb: After five wins and a lost season for the Commanders, McLaurin’s ADP is being punished in 2026 despite the fact that we saw only three total games where he played with Jayden Daniels. Remember how electric that combo was the previous year, and now see that you are receiving a whole round discount from what you paid last year. Our UDK stats have Terry as the clear target lead for a Washington team that sportsbooks project to have the sixth-highest average game total (48.1) in the NFL. Expect a ton of shootouts and expect Terry to recoup his cost as a draft-day value.

values.name: Chris Godwin Jr.
values.blurb: Godwin is not the sexiest name to click in your drafts. However, with Emeka Egbuka battling a toe issue, it would not shock us if Godwin is the clear target leader at the beginning of the season and a weekly PPR start. He will be the starting slot receiver for Baker Mayfield and a reliable FLEX option if you are looking for WR depth later in your draft.

values.name: Brenton Strange
values.blurb: If you miss out on elite TEs, we preach every year, ignoring the “middle round” trap at the position. Strange presents himself as a late-round value after he commanded a 16% target share in 2025. The hyper-athletic TE is in a contract year on a team that emphasized their need to run more 2TE sets this year. Second-round pick Nate Boerkircher profiles mainly as a blocking TE, while Strange is clearly the pass-catching weapon. Consider him a solid streamer with room to develop into a weekly starter.

values.name: Sam LaPorta
values.blurb: This is all about cost. Remember when LaPorta surprised every one as a rookie and was the TE1 in 2024? He was overpriced in 2025 and now it seems like the pendulum has swung back too far in the other direction. It is rare to be able to find TEs later in your draft with legit potential to finish in the double-digits in the TD department. The Lions offense could be a juggernaut and the team is favored in 14 of their first 15 games! LaPorta is circled in our drafts as a TE to target if you miss out on the elites early.
